To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) Sorting and highlighting total expected cost of health plans may increase the proportion of consumers who choose a plan with lower total expected costs.

(1) sorting health plans by total expected cost rather than premiums improved the choices of more vulnerable consumers (Experiment 1); (2) just in time education on the importance of total costs did not improve the sorting effect (Experiment 2); (3) sorting by total costs improved the choice of more vulnerable consumers in a more naturalistic choice setting in which future medical spending is unknown (Experiment 3); (4) just in time information increased the likelihood that consumers did not choose any plan
the choice architectures used in the ACA marketplace to present health plan information can be improved to increase the likelihood consumers choose the most cost-effective plan.
